children: Uganda and Rwanda are projected to post faster growth in their logistics and warehousing sectors than Kenya over the next five years, driven by rising trade volumes, infrastructure investments and the growing adoption of outsourced logistics services. While Kenya will remain East Africa’s largest logistics hub, the stronger growth rates in its neighbours signal a shift in where new demand across the region is emerging.

Research by Indian consulting firm Ken Research estimates that Kenya’s logistics and warehousing market was worth $6.34 billion in 2025 and will expand at an annual rate of 7.3 percent between 2026 and 2031.
Uganda’s market, valued at $3.18 billion in 2025, is forecast to grow by 7.5 percent annually, while Rwanda’s $1.12 billion market is expected to expand by 8 percent over the same period.
Kenya is expected to remain the region’s largest logistics market by a wide margin, but the faster growth rates in Uganda and Rwanda point to a growing shift in the sources of new logistics demand.

Pramod Bagalwadi, DHL’s vice-president for customs, transportation and warehouse management for the Middle East and Africa and acting chief executive for East Africa, said Kenya’s established position means growth in neighbouring markets could ultimately benefit Kenyan logistics operators as well.“From what I understand, if they start growing, automatically we start growing because we are helping them at the back end of the services,” Mr Bagalwadi said in an interview with The EastAfrican.“If they start having investments coming into their country, automatically that will be routed through Kenya as a hub, and if we can facilitate this growth, it helps us and it helps them.”Kenya’s advantage stems from its role as the main maritime gateway for much of East Africa. The Port of Mombasa handled 2.11 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in 2025, while the country has a large road, warehousing and freight-forwarding ecosystem centred on Nairobi and the Mombasa-Nairobi corridor. Ken Research estimates the Kenyan market could reach $9.7 billion by 2031.
Uganda and Rwanda, meanwhile, are building logistics capacity around markets that remain considerably smaller and more dependent on cross-border trade corridors.

Infrastructure development could provide an additional boost. Uganda is pursuing the 326-kilometre Malaba-Kampala standard gauge railway, which would connect the country more efficiently to Kenya’s Northern Corridor. The African Development Bank has committed to financing the project and has tentatively allocated about $650 million, subject to final financing arrangements.

Mr Bagalwadi said the development of rail and road links into Uganda’s hinterland could reduce logistics costs and encourage investment along the corridor.“If the rail system starts moving towards Kampala, then even the stretch from Kenya into the hinterland will start developing automatically,” he said.“The operating costs and import-export costs in those areas will become much more reasonable.”Rwanda has an even smaller logistics market but is forecast to grow faster than Kenya’s. Its position at the heart of the Great Lakes region, combined with access to both the Northern and Central corridors, gives it an opportunity to develop as a distribution hub for neighbouring markets.

The faster growth in the two countries is partly linked to their lower starting base, but Mr Bagalwadi said it also reflects deliberate efforts to improve trade facilitation.“Uganda and Rwanda were much more far-sighted, and they have done things in the interest of local industries,” he said, adding that cooperation with Kenya had helped make regional trade more seamless.
Kenya’s challenge, however, will be to convert its physical advantages into greater operational efficiency.

Mr Bagalwadi said the costs imposed on manufacturers and traders by infrastructure shortcomings can be significantly higher in East Africa than in developed markets. He estimated the costs associated with inadequate infrastructure at around 40 percent in East Africa, compared with 10 to 12 percent in Europe.“Today, I would say that infrastructure is growing, but making effective use of that infrastructure, managing it efficiently and ensuring it works optimally remain the key challenges,” he said.
As regional trade expands, addressing those inefficiencies will be increasingly important if Kenya is to maximise the benefits of growth in neighbouring markets.
